When you are "in someone's bad books," it means that person is unhappy, disappointed, or angry with you. They have a negative opinion of you right now, usually because of something you said or did (or forgot to do).

Think of it this way: imagine a person carrying an invisible notebook. In that notebook, they write the names of people they are pleased with on one page, and the names of people who have upset or disappointed them on another page. If your name ends up on the bad page, you are in their bad books.

It is a way of saying: "That person is not happy with me."
Simple Examples to Make It Crystal Clear

• "I forgot to call my mum on her birthday. Now I'm in her bad books."
    Your mother is upset with you.
  • "Don't submit your work late again, or you'll be in the manager's bad books."
    The manager will be displeased with you.
  • "He broke his friend's favourite mug and didn't apologise. He's been in his friend's bad books ever since."
    His friend is still angry with him.

Notice the pattern: something happened → someone got upset → that person is now in someone's bad books.
Where Does This Phrase Come From?

The phrase is rooted in a very real, historical practice. Centuries ago — particularly in medieval Europe — monasteries, institutions, and merchants kept actual written books or ledgers. These books were used to record important information about people: who behaved well, who owed money, who had broken a rule or caused trouble.

If your name was recorded in the section for wrongdoers or troublemakers, you were quite literally in the bad book. Over time, this very specific, physical idea became a figurative expression — meaning, it stopped referring to a real book and started being used loosely to describe any situation where someone is displeased with another person.

Eventually, the phrase evolved into the plural "bad books," which is the form we use today.
The Opposite Phrase: "In Someone's Good Books"

Every phrase like this has an opposite, and this one is wonderfully simple:

"In someone's good books" means the opposite — that person thinks well of you, is pleased with you, or approves of you.

  • "I stayed late to help my boss finish the project. I think I'm in her good books now."
    The boss is pleased with you.

So you can think of it like a scale:

  • Good books = that person likes what you've done ✅
  • Bad books = that person is unhappy with you ❌
How Is It Used in a Sentence? (Grammar Guide)

The phrase always follows this structure:

[Subject] + [be verb] + in + [person's] + bad books

Here are the different ways it can appear in tenses:

  • Present: "I am in her bad books." / "I'm in her bad books."
  • Past: "He was in the teacher's bad books all term."
  • Future: "If you do that, you'll be in their bad books."
  • Present Perfect: "She's been in his bad books since the argument last week."

You can also use it as a warning:

  • "Watch out — don't be in his bad books."
  • "Try not to get into the boss's bad books."
The Tone and Feel of This Phrase

This is an informal, conversational phrase. You would use it in everyday speech or casual writing — not in a formal essay or official document.

It has a slightly light-hearted tone, even though the situation it describes (someone being angry or disappointed with you) is not always pleasant. Native speakers sometimes use it with a touch of humour.

It is particularly popular in British English, but it is widely understood across all English-speaking countries.
Synonyms — Other Ways to Say the Same Thing

If you want to express the same idea with different words, here are some alternatives:

  • "In the doghouse" — very informal, same idea; someone is in trouble with another person.
  • "Out of favour" — slightly more formal; someone no longer has the approval of another.
  • "On someone's bad side" — you have made someone feel negatively toward you.
  • "In trouble with someone" — simple and direct.

All of these carry roughly the same meaning, but "in someone's bad books" has a unique charm because of its vivid, old-fashioned imagery of a literal book.
How Do You Get OUT of Someone's Bad Books?

This is a natural question! When you're in someone's bad books, you usually need to:

  1. Apologise sincerely for what you did.
  2. Make it right — fix the mistake or make amends.
  3. Give it time — sometimes, people need space to cool down.
  4. Show through actions (not just words) that you have changed or learned.

Once the person forgives you or approves of you again, you could say: "I'm back in her good books."

The beauty of this phrase is its simplicity: it paints a clear picture — someone has written your name on the "bad" page of their invisible notebook, and you need to earn your way back to the "good" page. Once you understand that image, the phrase will never confuse you again.
